lessons.title: Word of Mouth: Your Free Megaphone
lessons.summary: Happy customers are the cheapest advertising you will ever get. Learn how to make your product easy and fun to talk about, then give people a reason to share it.

sections.heading: Why people share
sections.body: People pass along things that make them look helpful, smart, or in-the-know. If your product solves a small annoying problem, or feels like a secret find, customers will want to tell friends about it. Your job is to make that story short enough to repeat in one breath.

sections.heading: Make it easy to talk about
sections.body:
- Pick one memorable thing (the "only" or "first" about you).
- Give it a name people can say out loud.
- Hand out something tangible: a sticker, a card, a sample to share.

sections.heading: Ask, and say thank you
sections.body: Most happy customers never think to recommend you until you ask. At the moment someone smiles about your product, ask: "Know anyone else who would like this?" Then thank them publicly or with a small perk. If you reward reviews or referrals, tell people clearly that the reviewer got something in return; honesty keeps trust high and follows advertising rules.

keyTakeaways: Referrals cost almost nothing
One memorable hook beats ten features
Ask at the happiest moment
Disclose any rewards for reviews
actionSteps: Write your one-breath description
Make 20 referral cards
Ask your next 5 customers for a referral

lessons.summary: Marketing to "everyone" is marketing to no one. Learn to describe one specific customer and go where they already hang out.

sections.heading: Draw your customer
sections.body: Picture one real person who would love your product. How old are they? What do they do on a Saturday? What bugs them that your product fixes? Write it down as a short character sketch and give them a name. Every flyer, post, and video should speak to that one person.

sections.heading: Go where they already are
sections.body: Instead of paying to bring people to you, show up where your customer already spends time: a school club, a community board, a local online group, a weekend market. List three places, then pick the one you can reach this week for free.

sections.heading: Test, listen, adjust

lessons.title: The 30-Second Pitch Video Formula
lessons.summary: A great short video has four beats: hook, problem, solution, call to action. Here is how to film one with just a phone.

sections.heading: Hook in 3 seconds
sections.body: Open with motion, a surprising question, or the product in action. If the first moment is a logo or "Hi, my name is…", viewers scroll away.

sections.heading: Problem → Solution → Proof
sections.body: Name the annoying problem your customer has, show your product solving it on camera, then add proof: a happy customer, a before/after, or a number.

sections.heading: Phone filming checklist
sections.body:
- Face a window for free, soft light.
- Hold the phone vertically for social, horizontally for screens.
- Get close: the product should fill the frame.
- Add captions; many people watch with the sound off.
- End with ONE clear action: "Visit us Saturday", "DM to order".

keyTakeaways: Hook fast
Show, don't tell
Captions on
One call to action

lessons.summary: Low-cost marketing still has rules. Learn the basics of truthful claims, disclosing paid endorsements, and respecting people's inboxes.

sections.heading: Claims must be true
sections.body: If you say "best", "fastest", or "100% natural", be ready to back it up. Specific, honest claims ("baked this morning") build more trust than big vague ones.

sections.heading: Email with permission

lessons.title: Honest Reviews That Bring Customers
lessons.summary: Reviews are often the last thing people check before buying. Learn how to collect real ones, respond like a pro, and stay on the right side of the FTC rule against fake reviews.

sections.heading: Why reviews matter so much
sections.body: A stranger trusts other customers more than they trust you. A handful of genuine reviews, even a few with small complaints, makes a new business feel safe to try. Your job is to make leaving a review easy for the people who already liked what you sell.

sections.heading: How to ask (the right way)
sections.body:
- Ask every customer, not only the ones you think will be happy.
- Ask soon after a good experience, while it is fresh.
- Make it one tap: a short link or QR code on the receipt, bag or thank-you message.
- Never offer a reward only for positive reviews. You may thank people for leaving a review, but not for leaving a *good* one.

sections.heading: What the FTC rule bans
sections.body: Since October 21, 2024, a U.S. federal rule bans buying or selling fake reviews and testimonials, including AI-written ones from people who never used the product. It also bans paying for reviews that must be positive (or negative), buying fake followers or views, and threatening people to remove bad reviews. Breaking it can mean serious fines.

sections.heading: Answer every review
sections.body: Thank happy customers by name. For a complaint, stay calm, apologize for the experience, and offer to fix it offline. Future customers read your replies too; a kind, helpful answer to a bad review can win more trust than a five-star one.

keyTakeaways: Ask every customer, make it one tap
Never pay for positive-only reviews
Fake reviews and fake followers are banned
Reply to good and bad reviews kindly
actionSteps: Make a short review link or QR code
Add it to receipts or thank-you messages
Reply to every review this week

quiz.question: Which of these is allowed?
options: Thanking everyone who leaves any honest review

quiz.question: How should you handle a negative review?
options: Reply politely and offer to fix the problem

lessons.title: Disclose Like a Pro: Ambassador & Influencer Rules
lessons.summary: If a brand gives you anything (money, free stuff, a discount, or you are its ambassador), your audience deserves to know. Here is exactly when, where and how to say it.

sections.heading: When you must disclose
sections.body: Disclose any connection that could change how people see your recommendation: being paid, getting free or discounted products, being a brand ambassador, working for the company, or being a friend or relative of the owner. A free product counts even if nobody asked you to post about it.

sections.heading: Where to put it
sections.body:
- In the post itself, where people will see it without clicking "more".
- Not hidden in a pile of hashtags, a bio or a profile page.
- In a video, say it out loud **and** show it on screen, not only in the description.
- In a live stream, repeat it from time to time for people who join late.
- On **every** post, because followers don't read them all.

sections.heading: What to say
sections.body: Use simple words anyone understands: "#ad", "Sponsored", "I'm a brand ambassador for this brand", or "Thanks to the company for the free sample". Vague tags like "#sp" or "#collab" are not enough.

sections.heading: Stay honest
sections.body: Only talk about products you have actually tried, share your real opinion, and never make claims you can't prove (like health or money results). Honest ambassadors keep their audience's trust and keep the brand out of trouble.

keyTakeaways: Free products count as a connection
Disclose in every post, where it's seen
Say it AND show it in videos
Use clear words like #ad or "brand ambassador"

sections.heading: Who can use it
sections.body: Google Business Profiles are for businesses that meet customers in person, at a shop or by visiting them (like a plumber or tutor). Online-only businesses aren't eligible, so they should focus on their website and social profiles instead.

sections.heading: Fill in the basics perfectly
sections.body:
- Correct name, address or service area, phone, website and hours (update them for holidays!).
- A clear description (under 750 characters) of what you offer and what makes you different, written for customers, not search engines.
- The right category; it decides which searches you show up in.

sections.heading: Photos and posts
sections.body: Add real photos: the outside of your shop (so people recognize it), the inside, your products and your team. Use Posts to share offers, events and news, each with one clear button like "Book", "Order" or "Call".

sections.heading: Learn from your numbers
sections.body: The profile shows how people found you (which words they searched) and what they did: calls, direction requests, website clicks. Check it monthly, then use those search words in your description and posts.

lessons.title: Build an Email List From Zero
lessons.summary: Social apps can change their rules overnight, but an email list is yours. Learn how to grow one with permission, write emails people open, and follow the CAN-SPAM rules.

sections.heading: Why email still wins
sections.body: Followers on social media see only some of your posts, and you don't control the platform. People on your email list chose to hear from you, and you can reach them directly when you have a new product, event or offer.

sections.heading: Grow it with permission
sections.body:
- Offer something useful for signing up: a tip sheet, early access, or a small first-order perk.
- Collect sign-ups everywhere you already are: checkout, events, your website, a QR code on your table.
- Only add people who said yes. Never buy lists or add contacts without asking.

sections.heading: Emails people actually open
sections.body: Write a short, specific subject line, one main message, and one button. Test one change at a time (two subject lines, or two send times) and compare how many people open and click. Keep what works.

sections.heading: The rules (CAN-SPAM)
sections.body: In the U.S., commercial emails must not use misleading subject lines or sender names, must include your business's physical address, and must give an easy way to unsubscribe, which you honor quickly.

keyTakeaways: Your list is an audience you own
Grow only with permission
One message, one button per email
Honest subject, address and unsubscribe link

lessons.title: Social Media That Sells (Without Paying for Ads)
lessons.summary: You don't need to be on every app. Pick one platform, post consistently, talk with people, and use social media to test ideas for free.

sections.heading: Pick one platform first
sections.body: Go where your customers already spend time. Teens and creators lean toward short video, local families often use community groups, and professionals use LinkedIn. Doing one platform well beats doing five badly.

sections.heading: A simple posting mix
sections.body:
- **Show**: the product in action or how it's made.
- **Teach**: a quick tip your customer will find useful.
- **Tell**: a real story, such as a happy customer (with permission) or behind the scenes.
- **Ask**: a question or poll so people reply.
Post on a steady schedule you can keep, like three times a week.

sections.heading: Be social, not just loud
sections.body: Reply to comments and messages quickly and kindly; social media is also a customer-service desk. Thank people who tag you, and share their posts (with permission).

sections.heading: Test ideas for free
sections.body: Want to try a new product, price or event? Post about it first and see how people react before spending money. Comments, saves and shares tell you what your audience cares about.

Show, teach, tell, ask
Reply to everyone

lessons.title: Track What Works: Links, UTMs & Simple Numbers
lessons.summary: If you can't measure it, you can't improve it. Learn to tag your links so you know exactly which post, flyer or ambassador brought each visitor.

sections.heading: What a UTM link is
sections.body: A UTM link is a normal link with labels added to the end, like `?utm_source=instagram&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=spring_sale`. When someone clicks it, website analytics tools (such as Google Analytics) record those labels, so you can see which campaign brought them.

sections.heading: The three labels to always use
sections.body:
- **utm_source**: where the click came from (instagram, flyer, newsletter).
- **utm_medium**: the type of channel (social, email, print).
- **utm_campaign**: the name of your campaign (spring_sale).
Optional labels like **utm_content** help you compare two versions, such as two different buttons in the same email.

sections.heading: Keep your labels tidy
sections.body: Labels are case-sensitive: "Instagram" and "instagram" show up as two different sources. Pick one lowercase spelling for each label, write them down in a shared list, and use a free URL builder so you never make typos.

sections.heading: Simple numbers to watch
sections.body: Follow the path from attention to action: how many people saw it, how many clicked, and how many bought or signed up. If many see but few click, improve the hook. If many click but few buy, improve the page or offer.

keyTakeaways: UTM labels show which campaign worked
Always set source, medium and campaign
Use consistent lowercase labels
Track seen → clicked → bought

Check results after one week

lessons.title: Your One-Page Marketing Plan
lessons.summary: Big companies write 50-page plans. You need one page: a goal, a customer, a message, three channels, a budget and a way to measure. Here is the template.

sections.heading: Start with one clear goal
sections.body: Make it specific and measurable, with a deadline: "Get 100 email sign-ups by June 30" or "Sell 50 bracelets at the spring fair". A clear goal tells you which ideas are worth your time.

sections.heading: Customer and message
sections.body: Write one sentence about who you are trying to reach, and one sentence about why they should choose you. Everything you create should repeat that message in different ways.

sections.heading: Pick three channels and a budget
sections.body:
- Choose up to three channels you can actually keep up with (for example: Instagram, an email list, and a flyer at the library).
- Write down your budget in money **and** time (2 hours a week counts!).
- Plan what you will post or do each week.

sections.heading: Measure and adjust
sections.body: Decide in advance what number you will check (sign-ups, sales, clicks) and when. Every two weeks, keep what works and drop what doesn't. A plan you update is better than a perfect plan you never look at again.

keyTakeaways: One specific, dated goal
One customer, one message
Max three channels you can sustain
Check numbers every two weeks

Set a reminder to review it in two weeks

lessons.title: Partner Up: Grow With Nearby Businesses & Creators
lessons.summary: Teaming up with a business or creator who serves the same customers (but doesn't compete with you) doubles your reach for free.

sections.heading: Find the right partner
sections.body: Look for someone with the same customers but a different product: a coffee shop and a bakery, a dog groomer and a pet photographer, a math tutor and a school supply store. List five possible partners near you or in your online community.

sections.heading: Simple partnership ideas
sections.body:

sections.heading: Make it fair and clear
sections.body: Agree on who does what, how long it runs, and how you will measure success (for example, separate codes or links for each partner). If either partner gets something of value for a recommendation, disclose it in public posts.

lessons.title: Pricing for Profit: Set Prices That Pay You
lessons.summary: Price is marketing too. It tells customers what your product is worth, and it decides whether your business survives. Learn the three professional pricing methods, how to find your break-even point, and why discounting is riskier than it looks.

sections.heading: Why pricing is a marketing decision
sections.body: Many new business owners pick a price by guessing, or by copying the cheapest competitor. That's risky. Your price sends a message: a very low price can say "budget" or even "low quality", while a confident price says "this is worth it". Price also decides how many sales you need to make a profit. If your price is too low, you can be busy every day and still lose money. Professional marketers decide on price on purpose, using numbers, and revisit it regularly.

sections.heading: Method 1: Cost-plus pricing
sections.body:
Start by adding up everything one unit costs you: materials, packaging, your time, and a share of your fixed costs (rent, tools, website, fees). Then add a markup on top. The key mistake to avoid is counting only materials. If a bracelet's beads cost $3 but you forget the 30 minutes it takes to make it, the bag it goes in and the card-reader fee, your "profit" is an illusion.

- List every cost per unit, including your time.
- Add a share of monthly fixed costs.
- Add a markup that leaves real profit.

sections.heading: Method 2: Value-based pricing
sections.body: Value-based pricing asks a different question: what is this worth to the customer? A handmade gift, a time-saving service or a product with a story can be worth much more than its cost. To find out, ask real people. Short surveys and conversations ("What would you expect to pay for this?") and looking at what similar products sell for give you a realistic range. Value pricing works best when you can clearly explain why yours is different.

sections.heading: Method 3: Competitive (market) pricing
sections.body:
Look at what competitors charge, then decide your position on purpose:

- **Premium**: higher price, justified by better quality, service or experience.
- **Market price**: similar to others, competing on convenience or relationship.
- **Discount**: lower price. This is hard for small businesses to sustain, because big companies can usually go lower than you.

Most professionals combine all three methods: cost-plus sets the floor, competitors show the market range, and value tells you how high you can go.

sections.heading: Know your break-even point
sections.body: Your break-even point is the number of sales you need to cover all your costs. The formula is simple: **fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit)**. For example, if your monthly fixed costs are $200 and each candle costs $6 to make and sells for $16, each sale contributes $10, so you need 20 sales a month just to break even. Sale 21 is your first real profit. Knowing this number makes every marketing decision clearer: you know exactly how many customers each campaign must bring in.

sections.heading: The hidden danger of discounts
sections.body:
Discounts feel like easy marketing, but they have costs. Frequent sales can teach customers to wait for the next discount, and they can lower how valuable your product feels. Very low prices can also start a price war you can't win. Better alternatives:

- Add value instead of cutting price (a free gift wrap, a bonus sample).
- Create bundles ("3 for $40") that raise the order size.
- Make limited offers truly limited, and honest.

sections.heading: Review prices regularly
sections.body: Costs change quietly: supplies get more expensive, platform fees rise, your time becomes more valuable. Put a reminder in your calendar every three months to recheck your costs and your break-even point. If you raise prices, explain the value honestly; loyal customers usually understand when you're open with them.

keyTakeaways: Price is part of your marketing message
Count every cost, including your time
Combine cost-plus, value and competitor pricing
Know your break-even number
Add value before you cut price
Recheck prices every few months

lessons.title: Keep the Customers You Win: Retention & Loyalty
lessons.summary: Getting a new customer takes effort and money. Keeping the right customers coming back is often the most profitable marketing there is. Learn how to choose who to keep, build loyalty without big budgets, and win back customers who drifted away.

sections.heading: Why retention matters
sections.body: Most beginners spend all their energy finding new customers. Professionals also ask: how many of our customers come back? Returning customers already trust you, need less convincing, and often recommend you to friends. Experts at Harvard Business School point out that the right level of customer loss ("churn") depends on your business model. A one-time product works differently from a subscription. But for most small businesses, a loyal group of repeat customers is the steadiest foundation you can build.

sections.heading: Keep the RIGHT customers
sections.body: Not every customer is a good fit. Some cost more time than they bring in, or want something you don't offer. Professionals decide up front who they serve best: the customers they can genuinely help, and who are valuable to the business. Then they focus their energy, offers and attention on those people. Write a short description of your ideal repeat customer and use it to guide your decisions.

sections.heading: The loyalty toolkit (low cost)
sections.body:
- **Remember people**: use names, remember preferences, send a thank-you note.
- **Make the first experience great**: the first purchase decides if there's a second one.
- **Stay in touch with permission**: an email list or follow, with useful updates (not spam).
- **Simple rewards**: a stamp card ("buy 9, get the 10th free") is cheap and effective.
- **Ask for feedback**: a two-question survey shows you care, and tells you what to fix.
- **Fix problems fast**: a well-handled complaint can create a more loyal customer than no problem at all.

sections.heading: Measure your repeat rate
sections.body:
You can't improve what you don't measure. Track two simple numbers every month:

- **Repeat rate**: of last month's customers, how many bought again?
- **Time between purchases**: how long until people come back?

If people usually return after about six weeks, a friendly reminder at week five ("New colours are in!") can bring them back right on time.

sections.heading: Win back customers who drifted away
sections.body: Customers who left aren't always lost for good. Research published in Harvard Business Review found that customers who came back to a service had a higher average lifetime value the second time ($1,410) than during their first stay ($1,262). The lesson: a respectful "we miss you" message, an honest explanation of what has improved, or an invitation to try something new can be well worth sending. Ask why they left, and fix it if you can.

sections.heading: Stay honest and respectful
sections.body: Loyalty is built on trust. Only message people who agreed to hear from you, make unsubscribing easy, and never invent fake urgency ("last chance!" when it isn't). If you offer a reward for reviews, follow the rules on honest reviews: reward people for reviewing, never only for positive reviews.

keyTakeaways: Returning customers are your most stable growth
Decide which customers you serve best
Small personal touches build loyalty
Track repeat rate and time between purchases
Win-back messages can be very valuable
Loyalty depends on honesty and permission

lessons.title: Be Found on Google: SEO Basics That Actually Work
lessons.summary: Search engine optimization (SEO) is how people find you when they search. There are no secret tricks. Google's own guidance says to make helpful pages for people, describe them clearly, and avoid spam. Here's how to apply that to a small business website.

sections.heading: What SEO really is
sections.body: When someone types "birthday cakes near me" or "how to choose a wool scarf", Google tries to show the most helpful pages. SEO means making your pages easy for Google to understand and genuinely useful for the people searching. Google publishes an official SEO Starter Guide for anyone who owns or promotes content, and it was refreshed in 2024. Its message is consistent: build for people first. Be wary of anyone promising "guaranteed #1 rankings": Google itself warns about this when hiring an SEO.

sections.heading: Think like your customer: search words
sections.body:
List the words real customers use, not your internal jargon. A bakery might call it "artisan levain", but customers search for "sourdough bread". Useful ways to find these words:

- Ask customers how they would search for you.
- Type your topic into Google and look at the suggestions.
- Later, Google Search Console shows the exact searches that brought people to your site.

sections.heading: Make each page clear
sections.body:
- **Page title**: a short, specific title for each page ("Handmade Wool Scarves in Portland").
- **Headings**: use clear headings that match what the section is about.
- **Readable web addresses**: /wool-scarves is clearer than /page?id=123.
- **Descriptive images**: give images meaningful file names and alt text. This also helps people who use screen readers.
- **One topic per page**: a page about gift boxes should be about gift boxes.

sections.heading: Write helpful, original content
sections.body: Google's guidance repeatedly comes back to helpful, people-first content. For a small business, that means answering the real questions customers ask: How long does delivery take? How do I care for this? Which size should I choose? A short FAQ page, a care guide or a "how to choose" article can bring in searches for months. Write it in your own words, from your own experience. Copying other sites doesn't help you and can hurt you.

sections.heading: Play by the rules: Search Essentials
sections.body:

- Stuffing pages with repeated keywords.
- Hidden text or misleading pages.
- Buying links or joining link schemes.
- Copying content from other sites.

The safe strategy is also the effective one: useful pages, honest information, and a site that works well on phones.

sections.heading: Measure with Search Console
sections.body: Google Search Console is a free tool that shows how your site appears in Google Search: which searches show your pages, how often people click, and any problems Google finds. Check it monthly. If a page appears often but few people click, improve its title. If people search for something you don't cover yet, consider writing a helpful page about it.

sections.heading: Local businesses: combine SEO with your Business Profile
sections.body: If you meet customers in person, your website and your free Google Business Profile work together. Keep your name, address and hours the same everywhere, link your profile to your website, and collect honest reviews. For local searches, these signals together help people choose you.

lessons.title: Video That Works: Google's ABCD Framework
lessons.summary: Google studied what makes video ads effective on YouTube and summed it up as the ABCDs: Attention, Branding, Connection, Direction. Here's how to use this professional framework for any short marketing video, whether it's an ad, a Reel or your Studio pitch.

sections.heading: Why a framework helps
sections.body: It's easy to film something that looks nice but doesn't sell. Google's ABCDs come from analysing what works in real YouTube ads, and they give you a checklist for every video you make. Google is clear that they are principles, not a formula. They help you check your ideas, but the creativity is still yours. Use them when you plan, and again before you post.

sections.heading: A is for Attention: win the first seconds
sections.body:
People decide almost instantly whether to keep watching. Google's playbook recommends grabbing attention early with pacing, tight framing and bold, high-contrast visuals, for example using two or more shots in the first five seconds.

- Open on motion or the product in action, not a logo or "Hi, my name is…"
- Frame close: faces and products should fill the screen.
- Start with a question, a surprise or a result.

sections.heading: B is for Branding: make it clear who this is
sections.body: A great video that nobody remembers you for doesn't help your business. Show your brand early and more than once: the product, the logo, the name. Google's research notes that a brand mentioned out loud by a person on screen tends to work better than a voice-over mention. So say your brand name yourself, naturally, in the video.

sections.heading: C is for Connection: make people feel something
sections.body: Facts tell; feelings sell. Use humour, surprise, a small story, or real emotion. Show real people using the product. And keep the message focused: one main idea per video. Google's guidance specifically warns against cramming in too much. If you have three messages, make three videos.

sections.heading: D is for Direction: tell people what to do
sections.body: Every video needs a clear call to action: visit, follow, order, sign up. Reinforce it two ways, by saying it out loud and by showing it on screen as text. Make it specific ("Order by Friday for weekend delivery") rather than vague ("Check us out").

sections.heading: Make versions for each screen
sections.body: People watch on phones held upright and on TVs and laptops held sideways. Google's recent guidance says both vertical (9:16) and horizontal (16:9) versions matter. Film with space around your subject so you can crop both, or make two edits. Try variations too: two different openings, then keep the one that performs better.

sections.heading: ABCD checklist before you post
sections.body:
- **A**: Does something interesting happen in the first 3–5 seconds?
- **B**: Is the brand shown and said early, and again later?
- **C**: Is there one clear idea, and a human or emotional moment?
- **D**: Is the call to action spoken and shown on screen?
- **Honesty**: If you're an ambassador or were paid, is the disclosure said and shown?

keyTakeaways: Attention: hook in the first seconds
Branding: show and say your brand early
Connection: one focused idea with real emotion
Direction: a specific call to action, said and shown
Make vertical and horizontal versions
Test two openings and keep the winner

lessons.title: Your First Small Ad Budget (Without Wasting It)
lessons.summary: Paid ads can speed up growth, but only if you control the spend. Learn how ad budgets really work on Google Ads (including why a day can cost double your daily budget), how to start small, and how to decide whether an ad paid for itself.

sections.heading: Free first, paid second
sections.body: Paid ads amplify what already works. They rarely fix a weak offer. Before spending money, make sure your free marketing is working: you know your customer, your message gets a reaction, and your website or shop turns visitors into buyers. Then a small, controlled ad budget can bring more of the right people to something already proven.

sections.heading: How "average daily budget" really works
sections.body:
In Google Ads, you set an **average daily budget**: roughly what you're comfortable spending per day, averaged over a month. Two details surprise beginners:

- On a single day, Google may spend **up to about twice** your average daily budget (a $10 budget can spend up to $20 on a busy day).
- Over a month, you won't be charged more than about **30.4 × your daily budget** (about $304 for a $10 budget).

So if you have a monthly amount in mind, divide it by 30.4 to get your daily budget.

sections.heading: Start small and focused
sections.body:
With a small budget, focus beats spreading out: splitting a small amount of money across many campaigns means none of them gets enough to learn what works. Start with one campaign:

- One product or offer.
- One clear audience or area (for example, your town).
- One goal: calls, visits, sign-ups or sales.

sections.heading: Watch automated bidding
sections.body: Automated "smart" bidding strategies can be powerful, but read the settings carefully. For example, Google notes that strategies like Maximize conversions try to spend your full average daily budget. So if you set the budget higher than you can truly afford, the system will use it. Always set the budget at an amount you're genuinely comfortable spending, and check spending in the first days.

sections.heading: Did the ad pay for itself?
sections.body:
Before launching, decide how you'll judge success. A simple professional check:

- **Cost per customer** = ad spend ÷ new customers from the ad.
- Compare it with the **profit** you make from a customer (see the Pricing for Profit lesson).

If an ad costs $50 and brings 5 customers who each bring $15 profit, you made $75 profit on $50: a win. Use tracked links (UTM tags) so you know which customers came from which ad.

sections.heading: Honest ads only
sections.body: Paid ads must follow the same truth-in-advertising rules as everything else: claims must be true and backed by evidence, and important conditions must be clear, not hidden in fine print. Also follow each ad platform's own policies. Never promise results you can't prove.

lessons.title: Truth in Advertising: Claims You Can Prove
lessons.summary: Honest marketing isn't just ethical. In the U.S. it's the law. Learn the FTC's core advertising rules in plain words: no misleading claims, evidence before you advertise, clear disclosures, and honest endorsements. Then use them to write confident, trustworthy marketing.

sections.heading: The three core rules
sections.body:
The Federal Trade Commission's guide for small businesses sums up U.S. advertising law in three ideas:

- **Ads must be truthful and not misleading.**
- **You need evidence for your claims before you make them.**
- **Ads can't be unfair.**

These apply to every kind of marketing: social posts, flyers, videos, emails, websites and ads.

sections.heading: What "misleading" means
sections.body: An ad can mislead by what it says or by what it leaves out. The FTC looks at whether a statement, or a missing piece of information, is likely to mislead a reasonable customer about something that matters to their decision. "100% natural" when it isn't, a "sale" price that was never the normal price, or hiding that a "free trial" turns into a paid subscription are all classic examples.

sections.heading: Evidence first
sections.body: Before you say it, be able to prove it. The FTC calls this having a "reasonable basis": objective evidence that backs up your claim. Simple claims ("handmade in small batches") need simple proof (it's true, and you can show it). Health, safety and performance claims need much stronger, often scientific, evidence. If you can't prove it, rewrite it as something true and specific: "customers say it's the coziest scarf they own" (only if they really did) instead of "the warmest scarf in the world".

sections.heading: Disclosures must be clear
sections.body: If a claim needs extra information to be accurate ("results vary", "while supplies last", "subscription renews monthly"), that information must be clear and easy to notice. Tiny fine print, fast-scrolling text or a note hidden behind a link usually doesn't fix a misleading main message. A good test: would a busy customer see and understand it before deciding?

sections.heading: Endorsements and reviews
sections.body: Testimonials must be real and reflect what customers typically experience. If someone was paid, got a free product, is an employee or a relative, or is a brand ambassador, that connection must be disclosed. And fake reviews (including AI-written ones) are banned under the FTC's 2024 rule.

sections.heading: Write confident AND honest copy
sections.body:
Honest doesn't mean boring. Strong, truthful copy is specific:

- Instead of "the best bakery", try "bread baked fresh every morning at 6am".
- Instead of "guaranteed results", try "here's what our last 20 customers said".
- Instead of "limited time!!!", give the real end date.

Specific truth beats vague hype, and it builds the trust that brings customers back.

sections.heading: Other rules may apply
sections.body: Every U.S. state has its own consumer-protection laws, and some products (like food, alcohol, credit or children's products) have extra rules. If you sell in a regulated area, check the specific rules or ask an expert. The FTC doesn't pre-approve ads, so it's your job to get them right.

keyTakeaways: Ads must be truthful, evidence-based and fair
Leaving things out can also mislead
Have proof before you make a claim
Disclosures must be clear, not fine print

lessons.title: Marketing Everyone Can Use: Accessible Content
lessons.summary: Many of your customers use screen readers, captions, zoom or high-contrast settings. Accessible marketing reaches more people, and it is simply good practice. Learn the essentials from the W3C (the organization behind web standards): alt text, captions, colour contrast, and clear design.

sections.heading: Why accessibility is great marketing
sections.body: Many potential customers use screen readers, captions, zoom, or high-contrast settings. If your posts, flyers and website don't work for them, you're shutting the door on real people. Accessible content is also clearer for everyone: captions help people watching in a quiet place, and good contrast helps anyone reading on a phone in sunlight. The World Wide Web Consortium's Web Accessibility Initiative (W3C WAI) publishes free, practical guidance.

sections.heading: Alt text: describe images that carry meaning
sections.body:
Alt text is a short written description of an image, read aloud by screen readers. W3C's guidance:

- **Informative images** (a product photo, a chart): describe what matters, concisely. "Blue hand-knitted wool scarf folded on a wooden table."
- **Decorative images** (a background swirl): give them empty alt text so screen readers skip them.
- Skip phrases like "image of" or "picture of"; screen readers already announce that it's an image.

Most social platforms let you add alt text when you post. Use it.

sections.heading: Images of text
sections.body: Flyers and promo graphics often put words inside an image. Screen readers can't read those words unless you add them as alt text or in the caption. W3C advises using real text instead of images of text where possible. When you must use an image of text, include the same words in the alt text or the post caption.

sections.heading: Captions for every video
sections.body: Add captions to your videos. They help people who are deaf or hard of hearing, and the many viewers who watch with the sound off. W3C explains that good captions include more than dialogue: important sound effects, music that matters to the meaning, and who is speaking. Keep caption lines short (W3C suggests one or two lines, generally under about 32 characters per line). Most platforms can auto-generate captions; always review them, because automatic captions make mistakes with names and product words. Also say important information out loud rather than only showing it, for people who can't see the screen.

sections.heading: Colour, contrast and clear design
sections.body:
- Use strong contrast between text and background (dark on light or light on dark).
- Don't rely on colour alone to show meaning ("items in red are on sale"); add a word or icon.
- Use readable font sizes and avoid long blocks of text in all capitals.
- Keep layouts simple, with one clear message per design.

W3C's "Easy Checks" page offers quick ways to spot common problems on web pages.

sections.heading: Plain language and clear links
sections.body: Write in short, simple sentences. Make link text describe where it goes ("See our gift guide") instead of "click here". Use emoji sparingly: screen readers read out each emoji's full name, so a string of ten emoji becomes a long, confusing sentence. Put hashtags at the end, and capitalize each word in multi-word hashtags (#HandmadeGifts), which screen readers can read more clearly. (These last tips are widely used social-media accessibility practice.)

Decorative images get empty alt text

lessons.title: Marketing & Children's Privacy: COPPA Basics
lessons.summary: If your business has a website or app that children under 13 might use, a U.S. law called COPPA applies. Learn what it covers, why photos and voice recordings count as personal information, and a responsible checklist for marketing that involves kids.

sections.heading: What COPPA is
sections.body: The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and the FTC's COPPA Rule protect children under 13 online. It applies to websites, apps and online services that are directed to children, and to general-audience services that actually know they are collecting personal information from a child. The FTC's "Complying with COPPA: Frequently Asked Questions" is the main official guide for businesses.

sections.heading: What counts as personal information
sections.body: It's broader than most people think. Beyond names and email addresses, the FTC's FAQ treats photos, videos and voice recordings of a child as personal information. That matters for marketing: a contest asking kids to upload a video, a "send us your drawing with your photo" campaign, or a sign-up form for a newsletter can all collect personal information from children. The Rule applies even when the child volunteers it.

sections.heading: Parental consent comes first
sections.body: In general, a covered service must get verifiable consent from a parent before collecting personal information from a child under 13, and must tell parents clearly what it collects and why. That's why Marketcraft requires anyone under 18 to use a parent's own account: the parent is the account holder and gives consent. For your own business, the simplest responsible approach is to market to parents, not directly to young children.

sections.heading: Third-party tools are your responsibility too
sections.body: Many websites and apps include outside tools: analytics, ads, chat widgets, video embeds. The FTC has reminded businesses that if they run a child-directed site or app, they must look into what every third-party tool collects through it. Choose tools carefully and turn off tracking and ad personalisation where children may be involved.

sections.heading: Keep only what you need
sections.body: Collect the minimum, and don't keep children's personal information longer than reasonably necessary for the purpose you collected it for. Delete it securely afterwards. If a business discovers it isn't complying, the first step is to stop collecting, using or sharing children's personal information until the problem is fixed.

sections.heading: A responsible checklist
sections.body:
- Aim your marketing at parents when your product is for children.
- Don't ask kids for names, photos, videos, voice or contact details without verified parental consent.
- Check every third-party tool on pages kids might visit.
- Keep data to a minimum and delete it when you're done.
- Use the FTC's six-step compliance plan if your site or app is directed to children.
- When in doubt, get expert advice.

Photos, video and voice of a child count as personal info
Get verifiable parental consent first

lessons.title: Build a Brand People Remember
lessons.summary: Your brand is the feeling people get when they think of you. Learn what a brand really is, how to choose a name, colours and fonts on purpose, and how to write a simple style guide so everything you make looks like it came from the same business.

sections.heading: A brand is more than a logo
sections.body: Many people think "brand" means "logo". A logo is only one piece. Your brand identity includes everything people see and hear from you: your name, logo, slogan, colours, fonts, symbols and the way you talk (your "voice"). Your brand as a whole is the reputation those pieces build over time. A small business with a simple logo but a friendly, reliable, consistent voice can have a stronger brand than one with an expensive logo and messy messages.

sections.heading: Start with your position
sections.body:
Before you design anything, write one sentence that explains who you serve and why you're different:

**"For [who], [business] is the [what] that [main benefit], because [reason to believe]."**

For example: "For busy parents, Sunny Snacks is the after-school snack box that's ready in 30 seconds, because every item is pre-portioned." Every colour, word and picture you choose later should support this sentence.

sections.heading: Choose colours on purpose
sections.body:
Colours carry feelings. Business guidance commonly links blue with calm and trust, green with nature and health, yellow with sunshine and happiness, and red with strong, energetic feelings. These are associations, not rules, so pick colours that match your position sentence and that your audience likes.

- Pick **one main colour** and **one or two supporting colours**.
- Write down the exact colour codes (hex codes like #6C4CF1) so you use the same shades every time.
- Check that text on your colours is easy to read.

sections.heading: A logo that works everywhere
sections.body: A good small-business logo is simple. It should still be recognisable when it's tiny (on a phone screen or a sticker) and when it's printed in plain black and white. Keep it to about two colours and one or two font styles: extra colours make printing more expensive and the logo harder to remember. Test your logo by shrinking it to the size of a thumbnail. If you can still tell what it is, it works.

sections.heading: Find your voice
sections.body: Your brand voice is your personality in words. Choose three words that describe how you sound, such as "friendly, clear, encouraging" or "calm, expert, honest". Then use them as a filter: before you post anything, ask "Does this sound friendly, clear and encouraging?" A consistent voice makes customers feel they know you, which builds trust.

sections.heading: Write a one-page style guide
sections.body:
A style guide keeps everything consistent, even when friends or family help you. It can be one page:

- Your position sentence
- Your logo and the smallest size it may be used
- Colour hex codes
- Your fonts (one for headings, one for text)
- Your three voice words, with a "we say / we don't say" example

Use the same colours, fonts and attitude on your signs, posts, flyers and packaging. Repeating them everywhere is what makes people remember you.

Pick 1 main colour and save the hex codes

lessons.title: Tell a Story That Sells (Honestly)
lessons.summary: People remember stories much better than lists of features. Learn a simple story structure for your business, how to make the customer the hero, and why the best brand stories are backed up by real actions.

sections.heading: Why stories work
sections.body: Our brains are built to follow stories with a challenge, a hero and a change. Research summarised in Harvard Business Review explains that people aren't purely logical decision-makers: feelings shape what we believe and what we do. A story lets a customer *feel* the problem and imagine the better ending, which a list of features rarely does.

sections.heading: Make the customer the hero
sections.body:
A common mistake is making your business the hero of every story. Customers care most about themselves. Try this structure:

1. **The hero**: your customer, and what they want.
2. **The problem**: what's getting in the way.
3. **The guide**: you, with a plan or product that helps.
4. **The ending**: what their life looks like after.

Example: "Maya wanted to bring something homemade to class but had no time on school mornings (problem). Our 5-minute muffin kit (guide) meant she arrived with warm muffins and a big smile (ending)."

sections.heading: Your origin story
sections.body: Customers also like to know why you started. A good origin story is short and true: the moment you noticed a problem, what you tried, and why you care. Keep it to three or four sentences on your website or profile. Details make it believable ("I spent my first summer testing 14 lemonade recipes on my neighbours"), and an honest small struggle makes it relatable.

sections.heading: Be a story-doer, not just a storyteller
sections.body: A Harvard Business Review article describes "storydoing" companies: businesses whose stories are proven by what they actually do, not only by what their ads say. For a small business that might mean really donating the part of each sale you promised, or really using the local ingredients you mention. When actions match the story, customers share it for you.

sections.heading: Keep it honest
sections.body: Stories are powerful, which is exactly why they must be true. A Harvard Business Review discussion of storytelling warns that because stories persuade indirectly, using them to sell carries a responsibility to be honest. Never invent customers, results or hardships. Real stories, even small ones, are more convincing and keep you on the right side of advertising law.

keyTakeaways: Stories make people feel, not just think
The customer is the hero; you are the guide
Short, specific origin stories build trust
Back your story up with real actions
Never invent stories or results

lessons.title: Market Research on a $0 Budget
lessons.summary: Before you spend money on marketing, find out who your customers are and who you're competing with. Learn free ways to size your market, study competitors, and run a quick SWOT analysis like a professional.

sections.heading: Two questions every business must answer
sections.body: The U.S. Small Business Administration describes two kinds of research that work together. **Market research** helps you find customers: who they are, how many there are, and what they want. **Competitive analysis** helps you stand out: who else serves those customers and how you can be different. Put the answers together and you find your competitive advantage.

sections.heading: Describe your customer in 3–5 traits
sections.body:
Professional planning tools ask for a short, specific description of your audience. Use both kinds of traits:

- **Demographics**: facts such as age group, location, income or business size.
- **Psychographics**: interests, values and habits, such as "cares about the environment" or "shops on their phone".

Then ask: is this group growing or shrinking? Where do they already buy similar things? How do they like to pay?

sections.heading: Free data you can use
sections.body:
You don't need to buy expensive reports. Government sites offer free statistics: the SBA's market research page links to tools such as Census Business Builder and data from the Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics. For a local business, also do "street research":

- Count how many people walk past a spot at different times.
- Read reviews of similar businesses to learn what customers love and complain about.
- Ask 10 potential customers three short questions (and listen more than you talk).

sections.heading: Direct and indirect competitors
sections.body: **Direct competitors** sell something similar to the same people (another cookie stall at the same market). **Indirect competitors** solve the same need differently (the café selling muffins). Make a simple table comparing 3–5 competitors on product, price, quality, location, customer service and reputation. Look for a gap: something customers want that nobody does well.

sections.heading: Run a SWOT analysis
sections.body:
A SWOT is a four-box summary professionals use everywhere:

- **Strengths**: what you do well (inside your control).
- **Weaknesses**: what you need to improve (inside your control).
- **Opportunities**: outside trends you can use (a new park opening nearby).
- **Threats**: outside risks (a big store selling the same thing).

Use strengths to grab opportunities, and fix weaknesses that threats could exploit.

sections.heading: Turn research into decisions

lessons.title: Map Your Customer Journey
lessons.summary: Customers don't buy in one step. They notice you, think about it, compare, decide, and (hopefully) come back. Learn the stages of the customer journey, what to do at each one, and which number to watch at each stage.

sections.heading: From stranger to fan
sections.body: A customer journey map is a simple diagram of the steps a customer goes through when dealing with your business. Harvard Business School Online explains that the stages often mirror the marketing "funnel": **awareness** (they find out you exist), **consideration** (they think about it and compare), and **decision** (they buy). Smart businesses add two more: **experience** (using what they bought) and **loyalty** (coming back and telling friends).

sections.heading: Different stages need different marketing
sections.body:
What works at one stage fails at another. A Harvard professor quoted by HBS Online stresses that the activity you need at each stage is very different:

- **Awareness**: be seen — posts, flyers, events, word of mouth.
- **Consideration**: answer questions — photos, prices, reviews, FAQs.
- **Decision**: make buying easy — clear call to action, simple checkout, reassurance.
- **Experience**: deliver on the promise — great product, quick help.
- **Loyalty**: stay in touch — thank-you notes, rewards, asking for referrals.

sections.heading: Find the "pain points"
sections.body: Walk through your own journey as if you were a customer, and write down every moment that's confusing, slow or annoying. Maybe your price isn't shown, or people must message you to find out where you are. Harvard Business Review describes journey maps as a tool for spotting exactly these problems so you can fix the experience. Each fix can bring more customers through to the next stage.

sections.heading: One number per stage
sections.body:
Pick a simple measure for each stage, so you know where customers are dropping off:

- Awareness: how many people saw your post or visited your stall.
- Consideration: how many asked a question or visited your page.
- Decision: how many bought (your conversion rate = buyers ÷ visitors).
- Loyalty: how many came back or referred a friend.

If lots of people visit but few buy, fix the decision stage before spending more on awareness.

sections.heading: Draw your map
sections.body: On one page, draw five columns (the stages). Under each, write: what the customer is doing, what they're thinking or feeling, where they meet you (the "touchpoint"), one pain point, and one improvement. Update the map whenever customers tell you something new.

lessons.title: Write Words People Actually Read
lessons.summary: Most people scan instead of reading. Learn what usability research says about how people read online, and how to write headlines, posts and product descriptions that get noticed in the first few seconds.

sections.heading: People scan, they don't read
sections.body: The Nielsen Norman Group, a respected research company that studies how people use websites, found that most people scan web pages instead of reading word by word. In one of their studies, 79% of test users always scanned new pages, and only 16% read word by word. On an average page, people read only about a fifth of the text. So your words must work even when someone only glances at them.

sections.heading: Put the most important thing first
sections.body:
Journalists use the "inverted pyramid": the conclusion goes first, then the details. Do the same: start with the benefit or the answer, not with a long introduction.

- ❌ "Welcome to our shop! We started in 2024 and we love baking…"
- ✅ "Fresh cookies delivered to your door in 30 minutes."

Research also shows people's eyes often move across the top of the content and then down the left side, so the first words of each line and heading matter most.

sections.heading: Make it scannable
sections.body:
Usability research found that making text concise, scannable and objective each improved how well people understood and used it — and combining all three improved it the most. In practice:

- Use clear headings that say what's below them.
- Use bullet lists for features and steps.
- Keep one idea per paragraph.
- Cut every word that doesn't help.
- Bold the few words that matter most.

sections.heading: Headlines: clear beats clever
sections.body:
People look at headlines first. Research found readers prefer straightforward headlines over cute or funny ones, because clever wording makes them work harder to understand. A great headline tells people what they get. Try formulas like:

- **Benefit + time**: "Learn to draw cartoons in one weekend"
- **Problem + solution**: "Tired of tangled earbuds? Meet the 2-second clip"
- **Number + promise**: "5 lunchbox ideas kids actually eat"

sections.heading: The first two words
sections.body: When people scan lists and links, they often only see the first two words or so. Start each bullet, button and subject line with the words that carry the meaning: "Free delivery on orders over $20" works better than "We are happy to offer free delivery…". Check your posts: if someone only saw the first two words of each line, would they understand?

sections.heading: Be objective and honest
sections.body: Hype words like "the best ever" or "amazing!!!" make readers trust you less, and the research above found that objective language helped people more than promotional language. Use specific facts instead: "Handmade in 3 days from 100% cotton" is more convincing than "the most amazing shirt ever". It also keeps your claims honest.

Put the most important thing first
Use headings, bullets and short paragraphs

lessons.title: Calls to Action & Pages That Convert
lessons.summary: A great post is wasted if people don't know what to do next. Learn how to write a clear call to action, and how to make the page people land on keep the promise your ad or post made.

sections.heading: What a call to action is
sections.body: A call to action (CTA) is the one thing you want people to do next: "Order now", "Book a free trial", "Visit our stall Saturday", "Reply YES to join". Every flyer, post, video and page should have one clear CTA. If you give people five choices, many choose nothing.

sections.heading: Writing a strong CTA
sections.body:
- **Start with an action verb**: Get, Book, Try, Join, Visit.
- **Say what they get**: "Get your free sample" beats "Click here".
- **Remove worry**: "No sign-up needed", "Cancel anytime" (only if true!).
- **Add a real reason to act now**: "Only 20 made this week" — but only if it's actually true. Fake urgency breaks trust and can break advertising law.

sections.heading: Keep the promise on the landing page
sections.body: The "landing page" is wherever people end up after they tap your link or ad. Google's advertising help explains that this page should repeat the ad's call to action and deliver exactly what the ad promised. If your ad says "Free tour", the page should show a big sign-up form for the free tour. If it says "Call us", show your phone number clearly. If it mentions a special offer, link straight to that offer — not your home page.

sections.heading: What makes a page useful
sections.body:
Google describes "landing page experience" as how relevant and useful your page is to the people who click. Useful pages:

- Clearly describe what the product or service does.
- Show prices and important details up front.
- Include honest reviews if you have them.
- Make it easy to contact you (phone, form or message button) without hunting.

sections.heading: Fast and phone-friendly
sections.body: Most people will see your page on a phone. Google's guidance recommends mobile-friendly pages and fast loading, because a slow page can be the difference between someone leaving and someone buying. Check your own page on a phone: Can you read it without zooming? Can you tap the button easily with a thumb? Does it load in a few seconds on mobile data?

sections.heading: No website? Use what you have
sections.body: You don't need an expensive website. A free Google Business Profile, a social media profile with a clear link, or a simple one-page site can be your landing page. Google even lets advertisers use a Business Profile as a landing page. What matters is that it's clear, up to date, and matches what your marketing promised.

lessons.title: Product Photos That Sell (With Just a Phone)
lessons.summary: Good photos do a lot of the selling for you, and a phone camera is enough. Learn the "hero shot", lighting with a window, backgrounds, angles and lifestyle photos, using the same standards big online shopping platforms ask for.

sections.heading: Why photos matter
sections.body: Online, customers can't touch your product, so photos have to answer their questions: What does it look like? How big is it? What colour is it really? Big shopping platforms take photos so seriously that Google's Merchant Center has detailed rules and best practices for product images. You can use the same standards for free.

sections.heading: The hero shot
sections.body: Your main photo (the "hero shot") should show the whole product clearly, on a plain white or light background, with the product filling most of the frame — Google suggests roughly 75–90%. For this main image, skip extra text, stickers, borders or watermarks: Google's guidance says added promotional text distracts shoppers, and it can get images rejected on its platform.

sections.heading: Free lighting: use a window
sections.body: Daylight from a window is the best free light. Put your product on a table next to a window (not in harsh direct sun), with a sheet of white paper or card on the other side to bounce light into the shadows. Turn off the room's yellow lights so colours stay true. Tap your phone screen on the product to focus, and clean the lens first!

sections.heading: Angles, details and size
sections.body:
After the hero shot, add extra photos that answer questions:

- Front, back and side views
- Close-ups of texture, stitching or ingredients
- Something for scale (a hand holding it)
- Each colour or style photographed separately, so customers see exactly what they'll get

Google recommends a separate image for every variant rather than one group photo.

sections.heading: Lifestyle photos
sections.body: Lifestyle photos show the product being used in real life: the backpack on a hiking trail, the candle glowing on a cosy shelf. They help people imagine owning it. Use them as extra images (not the main one). If people appear in your photos, get their permission, and for children get a parent's permission.

sections.heading: Size and honesty
sections.body: Take photos at your phone's highest quality; large, sharp images look better everywhere (Google recommends around 1500 × 1500 pixels or more for product images). Light edits for brightness are fine, but never change the product's real colour or hide flaws. Misleading photos lead to returns, bad reviews and broken trust. If you use AI to create or change images, be honest about it — some platforms require AI-generated images to be labelled.

lessons.title: Plan a Month of Content in One Afternoon
lessons.summary: Posting "whenever you remember" leads to silence. Learn how professionals plan content with themes, a calendar and a direction sheet, so you can create a whole month of posts in one sitting.

sections.heading: What content marketing is
sections.body: Content marketing means sharing useful, interesting or entertaining things — tips, how-tos, stories, behind-the-scenes videos — so people get to know and trust you before they buy. SCORE, a nonprofit that mentors small businesses, calls the content calendar a business's greatest organisational asset for doing this well.

sections.heading: Choose 3–4 content pillars
sections.body:
Pillars are the main themes you post about again and again. For a bakery they might be:

1. **Teach**: baking tips
2. **Show**: behind the scenes
3. **Prove**: customer reviews (real ones)
4. **Sell**: this week's specials

Rotate through your pillars so your feed isn't all "buy now". A common rule of thumb is to make most of your posts helpful or fun and only some of them direct sales.

sections.heading: Build the calendar
sections.body: Make a simple table with columns for date, pillar, topic, format (photo, video, carousel), channel, call to action and status. SCORE suggests planning one or two months ahead and working on each piece a couple of weeks before it goes live. Add holidays, school breaks and local events — content tied to the season is easy to plan and timely.

sections.heading: Use a direction sheet for bigger pieces
sections.body: For important content like a launch video, fill in a one-page "direction sheet" first: purpose, target audience, key message, call to action, format, channels, deadline and budget. SCORE offers a template for this. It stops you from creating something beautiful that has no clear job.

sections.heading: Batch it
sections.body:
Batching means doing the same kind of task all at once: write all the captions in one sitting, take all the photos in another, then schedule everything. It's faster and your posts look more consistent. One afternoon can produce a month of content.

- Hour 1: pick topics for the month
- Hour 2: write captions
- Hour 3: make images and short videos
- Hour 4: schedule and double-check

sections.heading: Learn from what worked
sections.body: At the end of each month, look at your top posts: what did they have in common — a topic, a format, a time of day? SCORE recommends analysing your past top performers and paying attention to what customers are looking for right now. Do more of what worked next month.

lessons.title: Win at Markets, Fairs & Local Events
lessons.summary: Farmers' markets, school fairs and community events put you face to face with hundreds of potential customers. Learn how to prepare weeks ahead, design a stall that stops people, and turn one-time visitors into returning customers.

sections.heading: Why in-person events work
sections.body: At an event, people can see, touch and taste what you sell, and meet you. That builds trust fast. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's farmers' market guides note that consistent, simple messages and good promotion bring people in. The SBA notes that many markets also welcome non-food makers such as candle, soap or jewellery sellers, depending on local rules — always check what your event allows, and whether you need a permit.

sections.heading: Start preparing weeks ahead
sections.body:
SCORE suggests starting to prepare for a major local event as much as 12 weeks ahead, with signs, updated online listings, posts and messages to existing customers. A simple countdown for a smaller event:

- **4+ weeks**: book your spot, check rules, plan stock.
- **2–3 weeks**: make signs and flyers; update your online profiles with the date.
- **1 week**: post a countdown; message existing customers.
- **Event day**: post a photo of your stall so followers can find you.

SCORE also found that during events, businesses that kept things fast and simple did better than those with complicated promotions.

sections.heading: Design a stall that stops people
sections.body:
You have about three seconds as people walk past. Make them count:

- A big, readable sign: your name and what you sell.
- Prices clearly shown, so people don't have to ask.
- Products at different heights (use boxes or crates) instead of flat on the table.
- Your brand colours on the tablecloth, sign and bags.
- A sample, demo or something to touch.

sections.heading: Flyers that work
sections.body: USDA's market toolkit advises that flyers clearly show the name, date, time and location. Keep one main message and one call to action. Give out flyers or cards with every purchase so people can find you again, and add a QR code that leads to your page or email sign-up.

sections.heading: Turn visitors into regulars
sections.body:
The real prize is the customer who comes back. At every event:

- Invite people to join your email list or follow you (with a sign-up sheet or QR code).
- Offer a "next visit" perk on your card.
- Team up with neighbouring stalls to recommend each other.
- Write down what sold well and what people asked for.

sections.heading: Adapt quickly
sections.body: USDA's lessons from running an evening market found that vendors who quickly adjusted to what customers responded to did significantly better. If one product flies off the table and another is ignored, move the popular one to the front, change a price, or try a new sample — during the event, not next month.

lessons.title: Customer Service Is Marketing
lessons.summary: Every time a customer needs help, you either win a fan or lose one. Learn what research says actually builds loyalty (hint: it's not over-the-top "wow" moments), and how to make getting help fast and easy.

sections.heading: The surprising research
sections.body: Many businesses try to "delight" customers with extra surprises. A well-known Harvard Business Review study of more than 75,000 people contacting customer service found that going above and beyond made surprisingly little difference to loyalty. What mattered most was how much **effort** customers had to put in to get their problem solved. The follow-up reported that 96% of customers with high-effort experiences became more disloyal, compared with 9% of those with low-effort experiences.

sections.heading: Reduce customer effort
sections.body:
Make getting help easy:

- **One contact, one fix**: solve it the first time, so they don't have to come back.
- **Don't make them repeat themselves**: keep notes on each customer's issue.
- **Be easy to reach**: show how to contact you on every page and package.
- **Answer common questions in advance**: a short FAQ saves everyone time.
- **Think one step ahead**: if a customer asks about delivery, also tell them how to track it.

sections.heading: A simple recovery recipe
sections.body:
When something goes wrong, a simple approach many businesses use is **LAST**:

1. **Listen** — let them explain without interrupting.
2. **Apologise** — sincerely, without blaming.
3. **Solve** — fix it quickly or offer a fair choice (replace, refund).
4. **Thank** — thank them for telling you; they've helped you improve.

Handled well, a problem can make customers trust you more, because they've seen you keep your word.

sections.heading: Measure effort
sections.body: The HBR researchers suggested a "Customer Effort Score": after you help someone, ask one question such as "How easy was it to get your problem solved?" on a 1–5 scale. If scores are low, look for the step that causes the most effort and fix it.

sections.heading: Not every moment should be effortless
sections.body: A later Harvard Business Review article adds balance: for some experiences, like a challenging fitness class or game, customers *want* a challenge or surprise. The lesson: make the boring parts (buying, getting help, returns) effortless, and save the excitement for the parts customers enjoy.

lessons.title: Handling Bad Reviews the Right Way
lessons.summary: Every business gets a bad review eventually. Learn how to respond calmly and professionally, what U.S. law says you must never do to hide negative reviews, and how to turn criticism into improvements.

sections.heading: Bad reviews aren't the end
sections.body: A business with only perfect reviews can look suspicious. A few honest negative reviews, answered well, show future customers that you're real and that you care. Many people read your reply as carefully as the review itself. Your goal isn't to "win" — it's to show everyone else how you treat customers.

sections.heading: How to reply
sections.body:
1. **Wait** until you're calm. Never reply angry.
2. **Thank** them for the feedback.
3. **Apologise** for their experience (even if you see it differently).
4. **Explain briefly** what you're doing to fix it — no excuses, no arguing.
5. **Take it offline**: invite them to contact you directly.

Example: "Thanks for telling us, Sam. We're sorry your order arrived late — that's not the experience we want. We've changed our delivery partner. Please message us so we can make it right."

sections.heading: What the law says you must not do
sections.body:
In the United States, the FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule took effect in October 2024. Among other things, it bans:

- Using **unfounded legal threats, intimidation or false accusations** to get a negative review removed.
- Showing only good reviews in a way that suggests they represent most reviews when bad ones were held back.
- Buying or writing **fake reviews**.

The FTC can seek large money penalties for violations, and it has already sent warning letters to companies.

sections.heading: No "gag clauses"
sections.body: Under the Consumer Review Fairness Act, a business can't put terms in its contracts or website terms that punish or fine customers for posting honest reviews. Customers have the right to share their honest opinion, positive or negative.

sections.heading: Reporting vs. hiding
sections.body: Review platforms let businesses flag reviews that are fake or break the site's rules (for example, spam or hate speech). The FTC warns not to misuse those tools to get rid of honest negative reviews. If a review is genuinely fake, report it with evidence. If it's honest but harsh, reply professionally.

sections.heading: Use criticism to improve
sections.body: Keep a simple list of every complaint. When the same problem shows up twice, fix it. Then tell people: "You told us our boxes were hard to open, so we redesigned them." Showing that you listen turns critics into fans and gives you great content.

lessons.title: Eco-Friendly Claims: Say Only What You Can Prove
lessons.summary: Customers love products that are better for the planet, so "green" words are tempting. Learn what the FTC's Green Guides say about environmental claims, why "eco-friendly" on its own is risky, and how to make specific, honest claims instead.

sections.heading: Why green claims need care
sections.body: Many shoppers want to buy products that are better for the environment. That makes environmental claims powerful — and easy to misuse. In the U.S., the FTC publishes the "Green Guides" to help marketers avoid environmental claims that mislead people. Misleading green claims can be treated as deceptive advertising.

sections.heading: Avoid vague words on their own
sections.body:
Broad words like "green", "eco-friendly" or "planet-safe" are risky, because the FTC says they're very hard (often impossible) to prove. Every product has some environmental impact. Instead, say exactly what the benefit is:

- ❌ "Eco-friendly packaging"
- ✅ "Packaging made from 80% recycled cardboard"

sections.heading: Recyclable and compostable
sections.body: "Recyclable" should only be used without explanation if recycling for that item is widely available to the people who buy it; the Green Guides use a benchmark of 60% of consumers or communities. Otherwise, add a clear qualifier, like "Check if recycling is available in your area." "Compostable" requires evidence that the whole item really breaks down into compost safely and in a reasonable time.

sections.heading: Comparisons and certifications
sections.body: If you say "less waste", say less than what: "20% less plastic than our previous bottle." If you show a certification seal, you still need to be able to prove every claim the seal suggests. And you must be able to back up every claim with evidence *before* you make it, not after someone asks.

sections.heading: Small businesses can still shine
sections.body: Honest, specific green claims are actually more convincing than vague ones. If you reuse jars, use local ingredients or deliver by bike, say exactly that, and show it in photos and videos. Customers trust what they can see. Keep a simple folder of proof: receipts, supplier details, test results.

lessons.title: Selling Online: Shipping, Refunds & Promises
lessons.summary: Selling online is exciting, but customers can't see you. Learn the rules for shipping promises in the U.S., how to handle delays and refunds fairly, and the basic "rules of the road" for advertising online.

sections.heading: Trust is everything online
sections.body: When someone buys from you online, they pay before they receive anything. Clear promises — what they'll get, when it arrives, what happens if something goes wrong — are some of the strongest marketing you have. Broken promises spread quickly through reviews. Under-promise and over-deliver.

sections.heading: The shipping rule
sections.body:
In the U.S., the FTC's Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule covers most products ordered online, by phone or by mail. Key points:

- If you say you'll ship within a certain time, you must have a reasonable basis to believe you can.
- If you don't state a time, you must reasonably expect to ship within **30 days**.
- That's why it's often called the "30-day rule".

sections.heading: When there's a delay
sections.body: If you can't ship on time, the rule says you must tell the customer and offer them a choice: agree to the delay or cancel and get a prompt refund. If you can't ship at all, cancel and refund promptly. You also can't swap in a noticeably different product unless the customer agrees first. Being upfront about delays usually earns sympathy instead of anger.

sections.heading: Clear policies build confidence
sections.body:
Write short, friendly policies and link them near your "Buy" button:

- **Shipping**: how long it takes to make and send, and the cost.
- **Returns/refunds**: whether you accept them, how, and how long.
- **Contact**: how to reach you if there's a problem.

Clear policies reduce questions and make hesitant customers more likely to buy.

sections.heading: Online advertising rules of the road
sections.body: The FTC's "Rules of the Road" guide explains that the same truth-in-advertising rules apply online as anywhere else: ads must be truthful, not misleading, and backed by evidence. Important information (like extra fees or conditions) must be clear and easy to notice — not hidden in tiny print or behind a link nobody clicks.

sections.heading: Under-18 sellers
sections.body: If you're under 18, check each platform's age rules: many selling and payment services set minimum ages for account holders. Make your online shop a family project — a parent manages the account and payments while you handle products and marketing.

keyTakeaways: Clear promises are strong marketing
Only promise shipping times you can meet
No stated time = ship within 30 days
Delays: tell customers and offer cancel + refund
Show shipping, return and contact policies clearly
Under 18? Sell with a parent's account
actionSteps: Write your shipping policy with a realistic time
Write your return/refund policy
Write a delay message template
Check your ads for hidden fees or fine print
