lessons.title: Protect Your Business From Scams & Hacks
lessons.summary: Small businesses and their social accounts are popular targets for scammers. Learn the most common tricks — fake invoices, phishing and account hijacking — and the simple habits that keep your business, followers and money safe.

sections.heading: Why marketers need security
sections.body: Your social media accounts, email list and website are business assets. If a scammer takes over your account, they can trick your followers and damage the trust you worked hard to build. The SBA and FTC both publish free guides because small businesses are frequent targets.

sections.heading: Fake invoices and "you owe us" scams
sections.body:
The FTC warns about fake bills for things you never ordered, such as website listings, "SEO services" or domain names, sometimes marked "past due" to rush you. Protect yourself:

- Check every bill against what you actually ordered.
- Limit who can approve payments (for a young seller: a parent).
- Search an unfamiliar company's name with the word "scam" or "complaint".
- Never pay anyone who demands gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency.

sections.heading: Spot phishing
sections.body:
Phishing messages pretend to be from a platform, bank or customer to steal your password. Warning signs:

- Urgent threats ("Your account will be deleted in 24 hours!")
- Links to strange web addresses
- Requests for passwords or codes

Never click the link. Instead, open the app or type the website address yourself to check. Real platforms won't ask for your password by message.

sections.heading: Lock down your accounts
sections.body:
- Use a **long, unique password** for every account; the FTC suggests at least 12 characters, and a passphrase of random words is easy to remember.
- Turn on **multi-factor authentication** (a code or app as a second step) everywhere it's offered.
- Keep a list of all your business accounts and who has access.
- Remove access for anyone who no longer helps you.

sections.heading: If something goes wrong
sections.body: Act quickly: change your password, turn on multi-factor authentication, and use the platform's account recovery tools. Warn your followers or customers through another channel so they don't fall for the scammer. In the U.S., you can report scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Young sellers should tell a parent or guardian right away.

keyTakeaways: Your accounts are business assets
Check every invoice; never pay by gift card
Don't click urgent links — go to the site yourself
Long unique passwords + multi-factor authentication
Keep an access list
Report scams and warn customers fast
actionSteps: Turn on multi-factor authentication on every business account
Make a list of your accounts and who can access them
Change any reused passwords
Save the FTC report link

lessons.title: Plan a Product Launch
lessons.summary: A launch is your chance to make a splash. Learn how to plan a launch in phases — before, during and after — with a timeline, a mix of free channels, and clear goals so you know whether it worked.

sections.heading: Why plan a launch?
sections.body: Putting something new up for sale without telling anyone is like throwing a party without invitations. A launch plan makes sure the right people hear about it at the right time. SBA's marketing plan guidance recommends writing down your goals, action plan and budget before you start, and SCORE's marketing plan guide walks through the same kind of planning step by step.

sections.heading: Set a clear goal
sections.body: Decide what success looks like, with a number and a date: "Sell 50 bracelets in the first two weeks" or "Get 100 people on the waiting list before launch day." A goal helps you choose the right activities and tells you afterwards whether the launch worked.

sections.heading: Phase 1: Before launch (2–4 weeks)
sections.body:
- **Test first**: let a few real customers try it and give feedback.
- **Build a waiting list**: an email sign-up or "notify me" message list.
- **Tease it**: behind-the-scenes photos, a countdown, a sneak peek.
- **Prepare everything**: photos, product description, prices, policies, stock.
- **Line up helpers**: friends, partners or local groups who'll share on launch day.

sections.heading: Phase 2: Launch day
sections.body: Make it an event: post across all your channels at once, email your waiting list first (they're your biggest fans), go live or post a video, and reply to every comment quickly. A real launch-only offer (like a free gift for the first 20 orders) gives people a reason to act now — but keep it honest and simple.

sections.heading: Choose your channel mix
sections.body: A good digital launch mixes several channels that support each other: your website or shop page, email to your list, social media posts and short videos, search (a complete Google Business Profile), and partners. You don't need all of them — pick the two or three where your customers already spend time, and do those well.

sections.heading: Phase 3: After launch
sections.body: The launch isn't over on day one. In the following weeks: thank your first customers, ask for honest reviews, share real customer photos (with permission), and compare results with your goal. Write down what worked and what didn't — your next launch will be even better.

keyTakeaways: A launch plan saves time and money
Set a goal with a number and a date
Before: test, waiting list, tease, prepare
Launch day: all channels, waiting list first
Pick 2–3 channels and do them well
After: thank, ask for reviews, measure

lessons.title: Test, Learn, Improve: A/B Testing for Beginners
lessons.summary: Professionals don't guess which headline or picture works best — they test. Learn how to run simple, fair A/B tests on posts, flyers and offers, read the results without fooling yourself, and keep improving.

sections.heading: What an A/B test is
sections.body: An A/B test compares two versions of something — version A and version B — to see which works better. Big advertising platforms build this in: Google Ads, for example, has an Experiments page that lets advertisers test a proposed change against the original and then apply the winner. You can use the same idea for free with posts, flyers, emails and signs.

sections.heading: Change one thing only
sections.body:
The most important rule: change **only one thing** between A and B. Google's own testing guidance recommends comparing versions that differ in just one variable. If you change the picture *and* the headline, you won't know which one made the difference. Good things to test:

- Headline wording
- Main photo
- Call to action ("Order now" vs "Get yours today")
- Price display or offer

sections.heading: Make it fair
sections.body: Both versions should get a similar chance: similar time of day, similar audience, similar number of people. Google's testing tools often split traffic 50/50 for this reason. For a market stall, you might use sign A on Saturday morning and sign B the next Saturday morning — not one on a rainy day and one on a sunny day.

sections.heading: Wait for enough results
sections.body: Small numbers can fool you. If 3 people clicked A and 5 clicked B, that could just be luck. Professional tools wait for a minimum amount of data before showing a result — Google's Demand Gen experiments, for instance, need at least 50 conversions per version when using conversion-based bidding. For small businesses: run tests long enough to get dozens of responses, and be careful about drawing big conclusions from tiny numbers.

sections.heading: Measure the right thing
sections.body: Choose your measure *before* the test: sales, sign-ups, messages or clicks. "Likes" are nice but don't always mean sales. Write down your guess (the "hypothesis") first: "I think a photo of someone using the product will get more orders than a plain product photo." Then see if you were right.

sections.heading: Keep a test log
sections.body: Keep a simple log: date, what you tested, version A, version B, results, winner and what you learned. Over months this becomes your own playbook of what works for your customers. USDA's experience with a night market found that vendors who adapted to what customers responded to did better — testing is how you find out what customers respond to.

keyTakeaways: A/B tests compare two versions
Change only one thing
Give both versions a fair chance
Wait for enough results
Decide what to measure first
Keep a test log
